steps.read: A long note on how the book was made: voice memos, a journalist agent, a librarian, ideas on a chapter map, and each chapter written by an agent from named sources. It says some chapters are honest placeholders and that notes to Dinis stay in.
steps.thought: Better than most: it admits the AI involvement up front, which answers half my question. But the other half, whether there is a person's thinking in here, is now a claim about a process, and I will test it. Also a lot of newsroom machinery I did not ask about.
steps.quote: The rule is simple: every number, every quotation and every story has to be in a source the chapter names.
steps.question: If the agents write the chapters from the author's articles, how much of the book is his thinking and how much is a rearrangement of it?
steps.confusion: It says this is not an official version and release candidate 2 came a few hours after candidate 1. I cannot tell how stable any of this is.
steps.next: Read on, but I am checking the sourcing rule against the chapters that make big claims.

steps.read: Five chapters before the argument: who it is for, why I am lucky, graphs, where I land, connecting the dots backwards.
steps.thought: A reading order promise. Fine, but five chapters of preamble in a 75,000 word book is a lot.
steps.question: Why does a book for a founder need a graph chapter before anything about a company?

steps.read: Two readers, Gen Z and Gen X, and the name ZX from the Spectrum. The stated objective is that by the end I have started a company, measured by how many companies come from the book. Cites a study of 2.7 million founders. Includes two notes addressed to Dinis in the body.
steps.thought: The ZX Spectrum paragraph landed, I typed those listings in. The stated objective is bold and testable, which I respect. But a book that promises I will have a company and covers the company in a chapter list I can already see is thin, I will check that. The age data suits me suspiciously well.
steps.quote: Our job is to empower the reader to create a startup by the end of the book.
steps.question: What is the 2.7 million founder study, who ran it, and does it say what he says about age 45 and industry tenure?
steps.confusion: I could not tell whether this is a second edition or a new book; the notes to Dinis say even he has not decided.
steps.next: Read the next chapter, then jump to the ones that make the claims.

steps.read: Wonder at what the author can now do, history of earlier technology waves, a dot-com crash paragraph, a pitch that technology finally works for you, and advice to read on paper with a pen.
steps.thought: I am looking for the thinking here and it is mostly mood. The fear essay he cites he could not read past the paywall, and he says so, which is honest but also means he is arguing with a headline. The dot-com line is true and not new. It is an upbeat chapter about feeling lucky, which an unemployed director is not in the mood for.
steps.quote: I could not get past the paywall, so I cannot tell you what it argued.
steps.question: What exactly is the fear he is answering, and who holds it, if the only evidence is an essay he did not read?
steps.confusion: The line that Gen Z had technology made to hook them and Gen X put the building down is asserted, not shown.
steps.next: Skim the graphs chapter, then go to the bold chapters. This is not where the book lives or dies.

steps.read: A graph is nodes and edges, a detective's board, Wardley maps as graphs with positions, nested graphs, and code as a layered graph with a story about an sgit commit reaching nine of 72 commands.
steps.thought: The code-as-layers section is the first idea I have not read in this form, and it is concrete. But it is also about his own tool, and the worked example is his own, unrun, hand-written stories. Interesting, not yet evidence.
steps.quote: That is a way of seeing, not a claim in physics.
steps.question: Does reading a diff at several altitudes find a bug a normal reviewer misses? One commit is an illustration.
steps.next: Jump to the founder chapter, the biggest claim in the contents.

steps.read: Expert founders beat the young outsider myth; Horsley Bridge venture return data; software people pay for and dislike; the Nokia inertia argument; explorer, villager and town planner code; and a closing pitch for a code review company built on layered graphs and the author's sgit tools.
steps.thought: The best chapter so far: sourced figures, a stated counter-argument, the Nokia point is a real thought, and he flags where his own articles contradict each other. But the ending is a business plan for his own product line, and the expert founders are two people he helps and himself. The solo-founder statistic and Stripe numbers are the fastest, not typical, which he admits.
steps.quote: I state this so it can be wrong.
steps.question: If the book is evidence the expert founder is the better bet, why are the three examples all people the author is connected to?
steps.confusion: Whether I should read the closing company as advice or as marketing; it is both.
steps.next: Now the chapters that are about his products, where I expect the selling.

steps.read: Zero-knowledge encrypted versioned vaults: sgit, read keys, write-only lanes, and why constraints drive good design. Includes two corrections to his own earlier claims, one about GDPR. Cites the EDPB and the ICO.
steps.thought: This is the strongest technical chapter and I was ready to hate it. The GDPR correction is what a careful person does and I believe it more for it. But it is the author's product, described at length, and the book keeps saying the chapter is not an advert. He does disclose the stake, and says nobody buys it for the encryption.
steps.quote: I have a stake here, sgit is mine, and the market will decide.
steps.question: What does sgit do that an encrypted git remote with age or a cloud KMS does not, in cost and effort to adopt?
steps.confusion: I lost the thread in the key management section between the vault key, read key, write key, append token and key pair.

steps.read: An agent has reach, a mandate and a gap; barriers are nothing, a prompt rule, a setting the agent controls, or something enforced above the agent; a proposal that vendors accept a behaviour policy as a third input. Aviation and payments liability analogies, then more about running agents.
steps.thought: The reach, mandate and gap framing is useful and I would use it. The claims I know to check: the prompt injection point is right and well cited. The proposal for vendors to accept a policy is a position, not a finding. And it reads as the sales page for a company: prices appear in ch 19, this chapter is the product.
steps.quote: I have a stake in it, and I say so.
steps.question: Who has actually run this on a real deployment other than the author, and what did the gap look like?
steps.confusion: Whether the five of seventeen rules example is real or invented; it says illustrative.
steps.next: Check how he handles evidence in the chapter about facts.

steps.read: Provenance, Popper, 'not found is not false', counting rather than remembering, and how his own memory was corrected by records: nine months was eight, 30 paying customers was ten.
steps.thought: The admission that an investor one-pager said 30 customers when the record says ten is the most trust-building thing in the book so far. Also the part where it explains the book's own method. Some of it is the generation-Z-are-detectives claim, which he labels as his experience.
steps.quote: In the last eight articles when I counted, five of my claims were confirmed, five corrected and two could not be found
steps.question: Is the corrected claim list visible somewhere, so I can see which were corrected?
steps.next: Go to funding, since that is the thing I am deciding on.

steps.read: Do not raise before profit; sell existing shares instead of issuing new ones, and lend part back; survivorship bias; an investor selection hypothesis about controllable founders; a UK worked example with tax; what breaks.
steps.thought: Genuinely a thought I had not read in this form, and he hands me the counter-evidence himself: Wasserman, Ewens and Marx, selection effects. The weak spot is the worked example, which is tax and securities structuring presented by a non-lawyer for a company worth 10 million. He disclaims it, but the chapter's whole thrust leans on an untested mechanism.
steps.quote: No study tests this model; the claim is from discipline and incentives, not data.
steps.question: Has anyone actually done a founder secondary plus subordinated loan on these terms, and what happened?
steps.confusion: How the fork, a possibility, is supposed to be an investor's insurance; the argument is a stretch.
steps.next: Last stop, the end of the book on how it was made.

steps.read: How the book was made: repository and vault, roles, articles as briefs, a review board with an advocate and a cutter, co-writing with Claude, the title decided twice in a day, and a request to email an address if I started a company.
steps.thought: I came to find out if this is a person's thinking. The answer given is: the ideas and decisions are his, the research and writing are the agents', under rules he wrote, and he shows the ratio. That is honest, and it is also the answer I feared: a lot of this prose is generated, and the chapters I liked are the ones with his voice and records. The last part is a book about its own machine. I have the picture.
steps.quote: The corrections I make are rarely to hallucinations; they are to briefs that needed to be better
steps.question: What would the book be if the process chapter were cut: is the book the process or the argument?
steps.confusion: The notes to Dinis and open questions in the last pages make it read as a working document, not a book I could buy.
steps.next: Put it down. I found what I came to find: it is more honest than I expected, but repetitive, partly a showcase of the author's products, and unfinished where it promises most.

steps.read: Wardley map, the four stages applied to many things, and explorer, villager and town planner as personalities, with a centre of gravity test.
steps.thought: The three-types idea is useful and sells itself. I can say which I am: town planner pretending to be a villager. The Myers-Briggs comparison is his experience, flagged.
steps.quote: Every dot is a claim. The positions are judgements, and the judgements are the argument.
steps.question: Does the book use the badges consistently?

steps.read: Connect the dots backwards, multidisciplinary people, a maths-teaching lament, learning with agents, and two of his pivots: Cyber Boardroom and MyFeeds.
steps.thought: A grab bag. The maths-teaching and fish-climbing-tree material is generic self-help and I know the Einstein attribution is false, which he admits. The pivot story is the real content.
steps.quote: Your future self will connect the dots. Your job now is to make dots worth connecting.
steps.question: Is this chapter about careers, learning, or pivots?
steps.confusion: It tries to be all three.

steps.read: A one paragraph introduction to the frame.
steps.thought: Fine.

steps.read: What generative AI is: buckets of AI, next word prediction, hallucination as a feature or bug, and the Starry Night image that clicked for him.
steps.thought: Plain and mostly right; the next-word explanation is better than most. Printed corrections from the model of his own claims are a nice touch. But I have read this several times.
steps.quote: Most of the trouble people have comes from asking for the second while set up for the first.

steps.read: A prompt is a lens, a role is a model with a description, an agent is a loop with a goal, and tools changed everything.
steps.thought: Sound, and the caveat that an agent is not just a loop is good. Familiar to anyone who has used coding agents for a year.
steps.quote: Good agents add planning, checks and limits; the loop is the skeleton, not the whole animal.

steps.read: Everyone who can brief an agent is a developer; spreadsheet error stories; Portuguese as the sixth most powerful programming language.
steps.thought: The spreadsheet horror stories are sourced and correct. The 'citizen developer is good news' claim skips that IT does have to clean it up. Repeats 'Execution just got cheap' from ch 1.
steps.quote: The citizen developer is the spreadsheet grown up.
steps.question: Who maintains what citizen developers build?

steps.read: Explorer coding versus vibe coding, why explorer code is not ready to be in line, and the handover.
steps.thought: The core distinction of the book and it is good. It also appears in ch 4, 7, 17 and 18; by now I have read it four times.
steps.quote: Explorer coding is not a way to ship. It is a way to find out.
steps.question: What is the handover in practice: a checklist, a contract?
steps.confusion: The handover is promised but remains a question to Dinis at the end.

steps.read: Short introduction to the job-hunting part.
steps.thought: Aimed at a different reader from me.

steps.read: Hired for the workflow: running agentic workflows is the competitive advantage, with a history of past rare skills.
steps.thought: The pattern of rare skills becoming normal is true. The assertion that the one answer in 2026 is running agentic workflows is a prediction presented as a conclusion.
steps.quote: Each of those skills later became normal.
steps.question: What would a hiring manager actually test for?

steps.read: Act as the job you want: do the work in public before you are hired; an unfinished section on the 2026 job hunt.
steps.thought: Reasonable advice that predates AI. The last section is an admitted placeholder, so the chapter ends on a hole.
steps.quote: The work gives you the CV you did not have.
steps.question: What about the interview process now?
steps.confusion: The placeholder section stops with nothing.

steps.read: Publish constantly; his Leanpub books stall; the voice memo to checked article loop; 148 messages and 65,323 words over 27 days.
steps.thought: The admission that his books stall is good. The recipe is concrete. But it is a chapter about running a newsroom, which is not obviously what a founder needs.
steps.quote: Small finished pieces beat big batches.

steps.read: A short introduction to working with agents.
steps.thought: Fine.

steps.read: A Google Drive and Claude workspace: one folder per contact with five documents and six lines of agent rules.
steps.thought: Practical and I like the Ledger, add-only. But it is a tutorial in the middle of the argument, and I see in the contents that it reappears as ch 30.
steps.quote: In a spreadsheet the record is the row, and the row is a summary you typed.
steps.question: Why is the same workflow in two places?
steps.confusion: I could not tell the two chapters apart.

steps.read: Agents as sessions with focus, one session per topic, writing lessons and debriefs, the brief as the unit of work, and a daily brief from a librarian agent.
steps.thought: Good practical content and matches my own experience. A few lines of this are the same as ch 7.
steps.quote: A thread is the model's frame of reference, and everything in it is context for the next answer.

steps.read: A short introduction to direction and judgement.
steps.thought: Fine.

steps.read: Direction is the scarce skill: places of highest leverage, and knowing when to stop.
steps.thought: The GUID randomness meeting is a true thing I have sat in. The core claim is reasonable and old. Someone who has managed engineers knows it.
steps.quote: Agents can build in any direction; what they cannot generate is the sense of what to build next, for whom, and when to stop.

steps.read: The centre of the edition, with a legal and tax disclaimer built in.
steps.thought: The disclaimer is sensible.

steps.read: Ship it, give it away briefly, take it away and ask if they miss it. Flags a tension with his own vibe coding wording.
steps.thought: Simple and a decent test, though not new: it is a form of the Sean Ellis test. The tension flagged with his own earlier article is honest.
steps.quote: If they shrug and go back to their day, you do not have a product yet.
steps.question: How many people is enough for the signal?
steps.confusion: The product testing story is told in two places.

steps.read: Four moves: define, price, deliver at linear cost, offer free to people who know you. RiskMandate's price ladder as the example.
steps.thought: It uses RiskMandate throughout as the example. It is the author's product and the early access programme. The review date in December is in the book, which dates it.
steps.quote: Price it first, because the price is the claim.
steps.question: Is the example the product's real performance or an illustration?
steps.confusion: The chapter closes with a review that has not happened yet.

steps.read: Sell by answering a question already in the room, and value that lands the day they switch, with a day on digital sovereignty.
steps.thought: The point that sovereignty and cost are important but not urgent is a real insight I have seen on registers. Again RiskMandate is the running example.
steps.quote: The reason to move must never be sovereignty, and it must never be cost reduction.
steps.question: What is the evidence beyond one conversation with one operator?

steps.read: A placeholder: the company in the UK, Portugal, Lithuania and the EU is not written, with a section on hiring through Upwork.
steps.thought: This is the chapter the book's objective depends on, and it is a placeholder with two lines. In the sold book this must be written or the promise has to go.
steps.quote: This chapter is a placeholder, and it says so.
steps.question: Where is the actual how-to?
steps.confusion: I expected to be told how to form a company and got a note.

steps.read: A short introduction to the serverless part.
steps.thought: Fine.

steps.read: What serverless means: an idle-cost table dated 18 October 2026 and the 'ephemeral town planner services' name.
steps.thought: The idle-cost test is sharp and useful: if it bills by the hour idle, it is not serverless. The table is a snapshot that will age. Mild whiff of renaming an established term.
steps.quote: I would rather replace the word than keep defending it.
steps.question: Who verified the prices?

steps.read: Open source: what it is not, the licence misconceptions, and the fork next door as investor insurance.
steps.thought: Mostly fine. The 'moat is a rate, not a wall' argument is an assertion. The 220-fork study with 7 merges is a real number.
steps.quote: Eight years on, everything in that chapter still holds, and the reason to do it has become clearer to me
steps.question: Does the fork next door work for a company whose customers are enterprises?

steps.read: Shipped means the user has it: a release that pushed cleanly and never reached users for forty minutes, and the fix of asking the live site what version it serves.
steps.thought: A concrete incident with a concrete fix, I like it, though it is a dev-ops chapter for people who already ship. The five-users plan at the end mentions a study; it is thin.
steps.quote: The checks were not weak. They were checking the wrong boundary.

steps.read: A short introduction to the long game.
steps.thought: Fine.

steps.read: Backup your life, graphs as memory, edges must be verbs, supersede never delete, and keeping a graph rather than getting it right.
steps.thought: The rules about edges are good practice. Repeats ch 3 and 16 on graphs and provenance.
steps.quote: You do not have to get the graph right. You have to maintain it.
steps.confusion: I found the graph material repeated across ch 3, 16 and 28.

steps.read: Civic responsibility: his 2010 and 2016 Lisbon talks, Hacking Portugal, what came true, and the state's plumbing.
steps.thought: Honest about what did not happen, which is rare. But this is a Portugal-specific chapter in a book for founders anywhere.
steps.quote: What I got wrong was the mechanism.
steps.question: Who is the reader outside Portugal?

steps.read: Eleven hands-on workflows dated 2026.
steps.thought: A good idea to separate the dated material.

steps.read: The same folder per person and six lines workflow as ch 13, in short form.
steps.thought: Close to a duplicate of chapter 13.
steps.quote: The difference is not the tool. It is what counts as the record.
steps.question: Why is it here and in ch 13?
steps.confusion: Duplicate.

steps.read: Build a first graph by hand in seven steps, starting from a question.
steps.thought: A real exercise. The warning not to pick a subject instead of a question is good practice.
steps.quote: A graph has no front page.

steps.read: Explain one idea five ways with a model, with the same lens argument as ch 7.
steps.thought: An hour exercise that repeats the argument it is practising. Thin.
steps.quote: It stops being magic. That is the point of understanding it.
steps.confusion: Repeats ch 7 including the maths example.

steps.read: Run an agent loop by hand with yourself as the harness.
steps.thought: A nice exercise for a newcomer; I know all of it. The final memory line is good.
steps.quote: Nothing is remembered by the model between sessions. Everything is remembered by the files.

steps.read: Storyboards as data drawn by Rough.js, a cast file and one file per story.
steps.thought: This is the site's own tooling and not what a founder needs. It reads as the author's project.
steps.quote: There is no image file to edit. Change the data and the picture changes.
steps.question: Who is this for?
steps.confusion: I could not tell why a founder would build this.

steps.read: Meeting briefs and follow-ups; says it is short on purpose because the sources are not there.
steps.thought: Another admitted placeholder, and it repeats ch 16.
steps.quote: This is a short chapter, on purpose.

steps.read: The recipe for a voice memo to checked site and an agent-worked inbox that never sends.
steps.thought: Concrete steps, including the rule that a failed check stops the release. Much of it appears in ch 12.
steps.quote: The house rules are the product.
steps.confusion: Overlaps ch 12 and ch 13.

steps.read: Form your company: not written, with what is known and what to decide first.
steps.thought: Second placeholder for the same promise as ch 22.
steps.quote: So this is the honest version: what the chapter will cover, the little the sources already say, and the decisions you can make before the steps arrive.
steps.question: Why two chapters for a missing one?

steps.read: A table of cloud and AI startup credit programmes as of 7 October 2026 with amounts and eligibility.
steps.thought: Useful and the most checkable page in the book, and it will be out of date in months. It says so.
steps.quote: A year from now several rows of the table above will be wrong
steps.question: Who pays for the book to be renewed each year?

steps.read: Price first, offer to people who know you, stop rule before the first message, count the results.
steps.thought: The same four moves as ch 19 in the same words, with the same RiskMandate example.
steps.quote: The research on paying first is not kind
steps.confusion: Repeats ch 19.

steps.read: A weekend build: static host, data in a vault, a model on the page, a payment link.
steps.thought: The most specific chapter and admits the 83 lines of server are an exception and have not run on a real account. Good honesty, weak foundation for a promise of a product by Sunday.
steps.quote: It has not run on a real account, does not do files over 4 MB and has one shared access token.
steps.question: Does a stranger actually pay through it?
steps.confusion: The product uses the author's vault service.

steps.read: Introduction to the process part.
steps.thought: Fine.

put_down.why: I came to hunt weak points and had what I needed: the chapters with the biggest claims are better sourced than I expected, but the book repeats itself, leans on the author's own products, and the final chapter is about the machine that made it.

buy_at_put_down.would_pay: nothing at £9.99 as it stands; about £9.99 if it were cut and finished
buy_at_put_down.why: There are ideas I had not read (ch 21, 25, 23) and it is honest, but the promised company chapters are missing, and I would be paying for repetition and product.

interview: A book for founders in the age of coding agents, in the author's voice, with the product-selling, process and tutorial material of a newsroom wrapped round a genuinely good middle on funding, shipping and agent control.

For the Gen Z graduate and for me, a Gen X expert. The parts for me are ch 17 on expert founders, ch 21 on funding, ch 24 and 25 on keys and agent control, and ch 27 on shipped. The job-hunting part (ch 10 to 12) and the storyboard and newsroom material (ch 34, 36, 41) are for someone else.

Mostly, because of the self-correction. Ch 16 admits 30 customers was ten and nine months was eight. Ch 24 corrects his own GDPR claim. Ch 21 lays out the evidence against his own thesis. What stopped me believing it fully: three of the chapters I liked are about his own products, and the ch 17 founder examples are people he helps.

Ch 2 lost me, it is mood. Ch 24 lost me in the key types. Ch 13 and ch 30 are the same chapter, and I stopped trusting the structure when I saw that. Ch 22 and 37 are placeholders for the very thing the title promises, forming a company.

It dragged in ch 2, 5 and 41, and in the hands-on part where ch 32, 33 and 39 repeat arguments already made in ch 7 and 19. It rushed the company itself, ch 22 and 37, where the promise is greatest and the text is smallest.

Merge 13 and 30, 19 and 39, 12 and 36, 7 and 32 and 33. Cut 34 from a founder book. Move ch 41 out to the website, keep one page. The hands-on part would be better folded into the chapter each exercise belongs to than set as an eleven chapter appendix that repeats them.

Ch 21 on funding by selling shares and lending back is the idea I would send round. The reach, mandate and gap model in ch 25 I would use tomorrow. The idle-cost test for serverless in ch 23 is a good one-liner. The Nokia inertia argument in ch 17.

The weakest are the placeholders (22, 35, 37), the duplicated workflow (13 and 30), and the notes to Dinis in the manuscript. Also the strong form of 'by the end of the book you have started a company' with no chapter that does it.

Parts of it read as a person: the tangents, the admission his books stall, the 2010 keynote that half came true. Parts read as an agent working from sources: the repeated 'In 2018 I wrote' openings, the habit of closing each chapter on a neat line, and the repetition of the same phrases ('Execution just got cheap', 'twenty years inside a problem'). He tells you it is co-written, which I respect, and it still reads about 60 percent person.

No, not at £9.99 in this form. At that price I would expect an edited book. If it were cut to 50,000 words, the placeholders written, the two overlapping chapters merged and the product examples diversified, I would pay £9.99 for the ebook and read it on my tablet.
Write the company chapters (22 and 37) from real steps, and cut the hands-on part to the chapters that do not repeat the argument.

Yes, two people: a Gen X friend who left a security vendor and is thinking about starting up, to read ch 21 and 25 only, and a former colleague who runs a small agent team, for ch 14 and 27. Not the whole book.
rating_why: A real person's honest thinking is in it and the middle chapters are good, but it is long, repeats itself, promises a company it does not tell you how to form, and keeps coming back to the author's products.

decision.why: Not in this form: the central promise has placeholders, the hands-on part repeats the argument, and I have the best of it from the free first edition and the chapters I read.

findings.what: The title and chapter 1 promise that by the end I have started a company, but the chapters that say how to form one (22 and 37) are placeholders, and the book offers a note instead of steps. The sold book cannot make this promise as it stands.
findings.quote: This chapter is a placeholder, and it says so.

findings.what: Several chapters say the same thing twice. Ch 13 and ch 30 are the same workflow, ch 19 and ch 39 the same four moves and the same RiskMandate example, ch 7 with ch 32 and ch 33, ch 12 with ch 36. A reader who notices stops trusting the structure and the length.
findings.quote: The difference is not the tool. It is what counts as the record.

findings.what: The practical examples for security, privacy, pricing and selling (ch 19, 20, 24, 25, 39) are all the author's own products, sgit and RiskMandate. The stake is disclosed, which helps, but a book that meant to teach me would use someone else's example at least once.
findings.quote: I have a stake in it, and I say so.

findings.what: The funding chapter argues for a sale of existing shares plus a lend-back, with a tax worked example, from a hypothesis that nobody has tested. The counter-evidence is fairly stated, but the chapter's confident close ('Do not get signed before you have the album') goes beyond its evidence.
findings.quote: No study tests this model; the claim is from discipline and incentives, not data.

findings.what: The case that expert founders win rests on a study of 2.7 million founders and three examples, two of them people the author helps and the third himself; it closes on a business plan for his own tools. It is sourced, but it is the book's thesis chapter.
findings.quote: I state this so it can be wrong.

findings.what: The last chapter and the notes marked For Dinis make the manuscript read as a working document. In the book that would be sold, the notes must go and the process (roles, board, candidates) shrinks to a page, or the reader ends on the machine and not the argument.
findings.quote: The corrections I make are rarely to hallucinations; they are to briefs that needed to be better

findings.what: The opening argument against fear rests on a Business Insider essay the author could not read past the paywall. It is honest about that, but the first chapter after the introduction is mood, and a reviewer notes it.
findings.quote: I could not get past the paywall, so I cannot tell you what it argued.

recommendations: Write chapters 22 and 37 as real steps for at least the UK, or change the title and the promise in chapter 1 to match what the book delivers.
Merge the duplicates: 13 into 30 (or the reverse), 19 into 39, 12 into 36, and 7 with 32 and 33, so the hands-on part shows the exercise and the argument chapter makes the claim once.
Cut the book towards 50,000 words; the 2018 edition was liked for being short, and the repeated openings 'In 2018 I wrote' and repeated phrases make this one feel padded.
Use at least one example for security, pricing and sales that is not the author's own product, or label the product chapters as case studies.
Remove the For Dinis notes and the placeholder sections from the sold book and shrink ch 41 to a page; move the process to the website.
Open the book with the funding and shipping argument (ch 17, 18, 21) and move the wonder chapter and the graphs chapter later.
Show the evidence behind the headline figures (the 2.7 million founder study, the Stripe median, the sgit commit example) in an appendix I can check from my tablet.
